opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the core intuition was that the world isn't text-only, and if you want a model that genuinely understands the world, you don't want to treat vision, audio, or video as an afterthought bolted on at the end.

The traditional approach was to train a strong language model, then attach a separate vision encoder and do some adapter training to connect them. That works reasonably well, but the modalities never really learn together. The language model's internal representations are already shaped around text, and you're asking it to accept a foreign input. When you train natively multimodal from the start, the model builds shared representations. Concepts in images, in speech, and in text all land in the same underlying space, and you get more transfer across modalities as a result.

There's also a data argument. We're increasingly thinking about where the next large sources of high-quality signal come from, and an enormous amount of human knowledge lives in video, diagrams, charts, scanned documents, and audio. If your model can natively consume all of that, you've opened up a much bigger pool of learning signal than text alone.

Then there's the practical side, which I think matters a lot for users. People want to point their phone at something and ask a question, drop in a long PDF full of figures, or have a model watch a video and reason about what happened. If multimodality is native, those interactions feel seamless rather than brittle. The model can reason jointly, so it's not just captioning an image and then thinking about the caption. It's actually thinking with the image.

To be honest, it's harder. You have more engineering complexity, more decisions about data mixtures, and more ways for things to go wrong at scale. But we felt fairly strongly that it was the right long-term bet, and the long-context work fits into this nicely. Being able to put an hour of video or a huge codebase plus screenshots into context and reason over all of it is where you start to see the payoff of having designed it that way from day one.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there were a couple of reasons, and they're kind of different in flavor.

The first one is just about the data. If you think about what intelligence is grounded in for humans, a huge amount of it is visual and auditory before it's ever linguistic. We learn what a cup is by seeing cups and holding cups, and then we attach a word to it. So if you're only training on text, you're training on this compressed, lossy description of the world that was written down by people who already understood the world. The model has to kind of reverse engineer physical reality from the descriptions. When you bring in images and video and audio from the beginning, you're giving the model a much more direct view of the thing the text was describing. And I think that helps even the text capability, which was a bit of a bet at the time, but I think it's borne out.

The second reason is more of an engineering and architecture point. There's a version of multimodality where you train a text model, you train a vision encoder, and you glue them together afterwards with some adapter. And that works, you can get reasonable results, but you've essentially got two systems that learned separate representations and now you're asking a small bridge to translate between them. When you train everything jointly from the start, the representations co-evolve. The model learns one internal language that spans text, images, and audio, and that makes things like reasoning over a chart or a diagram or following a video feel much more native rather than something bolted on.

And then the third thing, honestly, is where you think the product is going. If you believe that these models are going to end up as assistants that sit with you in your environment, looking at your screen, listening to you, watching what's happening, then text-only is just the wrong starting point. You'd have to retrofit everything. So it was partly a research bet and partly a bet on what people would actually want to do with it. It was more expensive and harder to get right early on, and there were definitely moments where you'd look at the text-only benchmarks and wonder if you were paying a tax for it. But I think it was the right call, and it's become table stakes now.

astra-6.text:
I think the basic intuition is that the world isn’t just text. We learn by seeing things, hearing things, interacting with things, and connecting those experiences. So if you want to build a broadly capable model, it makes sense for those different kinds of information to be part of its learning from the beginning.

Text is incredibly rich, but it’s also a compressed description of the world. If you’re trying to explain how something moves, for example, you can write a paragraph about it, or you can show a video. Those give you different kinds of information. Having a model learn across both gives it an opportunity to connect the language to what’s actually happening.

And I think that’s the deeper motivation: you want those capabilities to reinforce one another. You want what the model learns from language to help it understand an image, and what it learns visually to help it reason about a question expressed in language. Building around that from the start is a very natural design choice.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the core reason is that the world isn’t just text. Text is an incredibly useful representation of what people know, but there’s so much information in what we see and hear that doesn’t naturally get written down. If you want a model to develop a broad understanding of the world, it makes sense to let it learn from all of those sources together.

And those modalities can help each other. You might learn a concept through language, then see how it actually plays out in a video. Or something that’s ambiguous in an image becomes clear when you hear the accompanying audio. Training them together gives the model an opportunity to discover those connections, rather than having us build separate systems and then try to stitch their understanding together afterward.

It also makes the interaction much more natural. You can show the model what you’re looking at and ask a question about it. That feels like a fairly fundamental capability for a general-purpose assistant, so designing for it from the beginning seemed like the right direction.
